title: Choosing a data store
summary: The data store is the decision a design cannot easily revisit. This lesson reads an access pattern into a kind of store, puts eight criteria against relational, key-value, wide-column, document, search, time-series, graph and object stores in one decision, explains the guarantees that separate them, prices the case where one store is not enough, warns about the migration a wrong choice forces, maps each kind to its AWS managed service from the AWS database decision guide, and walks the news feed through the whole choice.

blocks.text: Amazon built Dynamo, and later DynamoDB, because it measured its own access patterns: about 70 percent of operations were key-value lookups by primary key returning one row, and services such as the shopping cart needed a store that stayed writeable through disk, network and data-centre failures. The Dynamo paper lists the services that need only primary-key access and states that a relational database would have limited their scale and availability.

blocks.text: Discord's search is a derived store by design: Elasticsearch was chosen over Solr for its self-contained discovery and automatic shard rebalancing, messages are indexed lazily only when a server is first searched, and the mapping from servers to index shards is stored in Cassandra, the primary store, as the source of truth with a cache in front of it.

Stripe migrated hundreds of millions of Subscriptions objects to a new data model with every service at full traffic, using the four-step dual-writing pattern: dual write to the existing and new tables and backfill the history, change every read path to the new table, change every write path to write only to the new table, then remove the old data that relies on the outdated model.

subtopics.title: Why the data store is the decision

blocks.text: Most architecture decisions can be revisited in a sprint. The data store cannot: it fixes the data model, the queries that are cheap, the guarantees the application may assume, and the migration that will one day be needed to leave it. For decades the choice was not made at all, because the only option was a relational database and every application's data was modelled as relational whether it fitted or not; Werner Vogels's account of why Amazon built purpose-built stores makes the point that the database was driving the data model rather than the use case driving the database.

The original evidence is in the same account and in the Dynamo paper. Amazon found that about 70 percent of its operations were key-value lookups that used only a primary key and returned a single row, and the paper lists the services that need only primary-key access, from shopping carts to session management and best-seller lists, for which a relational database would limit scale and availability. A store that offers only that access path can promise what those services need, including staying writeable while disks fail and network routes flap.

blocks.caption: The eight kinds of store this lesson chooses between, by the shape of the question each answers best.
rows: rows in tables with a schema
any query over several tables, with transactions and joins
get or put one item by key, at any scale
rows grouped in a partition, sorted by a clustering key
a range within one partition, writes at high rate
fetch or update one document and query its fields
an inverted index over text and fields
full-text and faceted search, relevance ranking
samples labelled by metric and tags
put and get large blobs cheaply and durably
Amazon S3 and other object stores

blocks.text: The lesson on storage engines explained the mechanism under each kind; this lesson is about the choice. It reads an access pattern into a store kind, puts the criteria against the kinds in one decision, prices the case where one store is not enough, warns about the migration that a wrong choice forces, and maps each kind to the managed service that runs it on AWS. The worked example walks the news feed from this module through the decision.
Choose the store from the queries, not from the data. Two products with the same entities but different questions belong on different stores; the questions are what the store has to make cheap.

subtopics.title: Reading an access pattern into a store

blocks.text: The DynamoDB design guide states the discipline for every non-relational store in one sentence: do not start designing the schema until you know the questions it will need to answer. A relational schema can be normalised first and queried later; a key-value, wide-column or document schema is the queries, so the queries come first. Cassandra's documentation says the same of its model: modelling is query-driven, each query is best served by a single table, and entities are duplicated across tables to make that true.

blocks.title: Writing down an access pattern
items: List every read and write the product makes, as a sentence: fetch a user's timeline, append a post to each follower's timeline, search posts by text.
For each one, name the key it arrives with: a user id, a post id, a text query, a time range. A query with no key is a scan or a search, which alone narrows the store.
Estimate its peak rate per second and the size of what it reads or writes.
State what it must see: its own last write, every write before it, or anything recent.
Mark the ones that must happen together or not at all. Those are the transactions, and they decide whether one store can hold the data.
Sort by rate times size. The top two or three are the dominant paths; the store is chosen for them.

blocks.text: The DynamoDB guide names three properties to know before modelling: the size of the data stored and requested at once, its shape, and its velocity. Those three plus the consistency need sort most patterns into a kind. A key with a small value at a high rate is key-value. A key that owns a growing sorted list is wide-column. A text query is a search index. A time range over labelled samples is time series. A question that walks relationships several hops deep is a graph. A question that joins entities in ways nobody predicted is relational, and so is any set of writes that must be atomic across entities.

blocks.caption: The news feed's access patterns, as the next steps need them. Rates are the estimates from the news feed exercise in this module (assumptions, not measurements).
rows: a sorted list per key: wide-column or an in-memory list
append a post to each follower's timeline
the same list per key, write-heavy
list who I follow and who follows me

blocks.text: The pattern missing from the list is the one that forces the second store or the migration. Ask for the reporting queries, the admin screens and the search box before choosing; a key-value model cannot answer them.

subtopics.title: The decision: which store for which workload

blocks.text: The decision block is the centre of the lesson: one row per kind of store, the workload it is built for, the workload that breaks it, and named examples with the AWS managed service after them, mapped from the AWS database decision guide and taken up again at the end.

blocks.caption: Choosing a data store. Products are examples of the kind; the AWS service after the semicolon follows the decision guide, except S3, which the guide does not cover.

rows.pick_when: queries are varied and will change, writes must be atomic across entities, and the data fits one primary with replicas, which is most products
rows.avoid_when: the dominant path is a single-key lookup at a rate one primary cannot serve, or a sorted list per key that grows without bound
rows.example: PostgreSQL, MySQL; Aurora or RDS, Aurora DSQL for multi-region

rows.pick_when: almost every access is get or put by a known key, the rate or size is beyond one machine, and the store must stay writeable through failures
rows.avoid_when: the product needs ad hoc queries, joins or transactions across many items, or the questions are not yet known

rows.pick_when: each key owns a sorted, growing list read by range, writes dominate, and the partition can be bounded, as a chat channel or a timeline is
rows.avoid_when: queries cross partitions, a partition can become hot, or the team has nobody to run the cluster

rows.pick_when: each entity is read and written whole, its fields vary by record, and queries are on the fields of one document
rows.avoid_when: data is relational underneath and the joins are hidden in application code, or multi-document transactions are common
rows.example: MongoDB; DocumentDB, or jsonb columns in PostgreSQL

rows.pick_when: the question is a text query or a faceted filter ranked by relevance, over data owned by another store
rows.avoid_when: it would be the only copy of the data; it is a derived index and must be rebuildable

rows.pick_when: samples arrive at a high rate with a timestamp and labels, are queried by range and aggregated, and age out
rows.avoid_when: every sample must be exact and complete, as for per-request billing, or the queries are not over time

rows.pick_when: the questions traverse many relationships several hops deep: fraud rings, social paths, recommendations, knowledge graphs
rows.avoid_when: the graph is shallow and the questions are one hop, which a join or a key lookup answers

rows.pick_when: objects are large, written once, read whole or by range, and durability per byte must be cheap
rows.avoid_when: the application needs small updates, listing by attributes or transactions across objects; keep those in a metadata store
rows.example: Amazon S3 and other object stores; S3

blocks.text: Start from relational unless a dominant path proves otherwise. Leave it for a key-value or wide-column store when one path's rate or growth exceeds one primary; add a search, time-series or graph store beside it when a question has that shape; never let a derived store become the only copy.

The decision rows compress eight criteria. The two tables expand them so that a reviewer can disagree with one cell rather than a row; the cells follow the AWS decision guide, the vendor documentation cited in the captions, and the mechanism taught in the storage-engines lesson.

fields of one document; secondary indexes

put and get whole objects, range reads
near real time; a derived copy
approximate is acceptable; not for billing
opaque bytes with a few metadata fields

blocks.text: Two cells deserve a sentence, and one row a caveat: the team-familiarity row is the lesson's own judgement, not a source's. Query flexibility is the hidden price of every non-relational choice: the DynamoDB guide describes data that can be queried efficiently in a limited number of ways, outside of which queries are expensive, against relational data that can be queried flexibly at a cost that does not scale under high traffic. The time-series consistency cell is the Prometheus project's own warning: where every sample must be exact, as in per-request billing, another store must hold the record.

subtopics.title: Guarantees, transactions and the shape of the answer

blocks.text: Three guarantees separate the kinds more sharply than throughput does. The first is atomicity across entities: a relational store commits several rows in one transaction as a matter of course, while a key-value or document store makes a single item the unit of atomicity and offers cross-item transactions, where it offers them at all, as a bounded special case. A product whose core operation moves value between two records, a ledger or an inventory, has this guarantee as its dominant path.

The second is what a read may see. The Dynamo paper's design target is an always-writeable store: a shopping cart must accept an add even while servers and network paths fail, and the price is that two replicas may hold divergent versions to be reconciled later. The relational default is the opposite: one primary accepts writes and a read on it sees every committed write. Neither is better; the question is which failure the product would rather have, a rejected write or a stale read.

The third is exactness of the answer. A search index ranks by relevance, which is a judgement rather than a match; a vector index returns approximate neighbours, and pgvector's documentation states the trade plainly: exact search by default with perfect recall, or an approximate index, HNSW or IVFFlat, that trades some recall for speed and changes the results a query returns. A time-series store may drop or round samples by design. Each is the right answer for its question and the wrong one for a question that needs the exact row.

blocks.caption: What each kind promises, and what a product must not ask of it.
rows: a transaction over many rows and tables
every committed write, on the primary
one item or document; bounded multi-item transactions where offered
configurable; eventually consistent reads are the cheap default in many stores
approximate unless exact search is chosen
approximate by design in monitoring stores

blocks.text: Put the guarantee next to the query when sorting patterns. A query that needs atomicity across entities or an exact, strongly consistent answer stays on the relational store even if its rate would fit a cheaper one.

subtopics.title: When one store is not enough, and what two cost

blocks.text: Most products end up with a primary store plus derived ones: a cache for the hot reads, a search index for the text queries, a time-series store for the metrics, an analytics copy for the reports, an object store for the files. The rule that keeps this sane is that exactly one of them is the source of truth and every other is rebuildable from it. Discord's search is the pattern done right: messages live in Cassandra, Elasticsearch holds an index that is built lazily, only when someone first searches a server, and even the mapping of servers to index shards is kept in Cassandra as the source of truth with the index as a derived copy.

blocks.caption: What a second store adds and what it costs.
rows: invalidation, cold starts, a stale-read story
a pipeline that feeds it, a lag, and a reindex when the mapping changes
metrics over time at high ingest
retention policy, cardinality limits, a second query language
a batch or change-data pipeline and a freshness lag
a metadata table to keep in step; orphaned objects
the right shape for one query
two systems to run, two failure modes, two skill sets, and a dual-write path that can disagree

blocks.text: The cost is rarely in the software. It is in the pipeline between the stores, which is a second write path that can fail half-way; in the lag, which the product must tolerate and the support team must explain; in the on-call surface, which doubles; and in the people, since each kind of store has its own failure modes and tuning. The AWS decision guide's advice on vector search generalises: a team that already runs a hundred PostgreSQL databases should first evaluate the vector extension on the engine it knows, because the same engine lets developers use the skills and tools they have rather than learn a new system.

So the second store has to earn its place with a query the first cannot serve at the required rate or shape, not with a preference. The order of preference is: the primary store's own feature, such as a JSON column, full-text search or a vector extension in PostgreSQL; a managed derived store fed by change capture; and only then a second primary with its own writes.

Two sources of truth is the expensive mistake. If the application writes the same fact to two stores directly, every failure between the two writes leaves them disagreeing, and no rebuild can decide which is right. Derive the second store from the first, through its log or change stream, so that the first can always regenerate it.

The wrong store is not discovered at design time; it is discovered when the dataset outgrows it, and leaving it then means migrating live data under full traffic. Discord's message store shows both halves. The first version was a single MongoDB replica set, chosen for speed of iteration, and the team planned from the start for an easy migration out. At about 100 million messages the data and its index no longer fitted in RAM, latency became unpredictable, and the messages moved to Cassandra with a partition key of channel and time bucket sized to stay under 100 MB. Six years later the Cassandra cluster had grown from 12 nodes to 177, was high toil with hot partitions that hurt the whole cluster, and was migrated again, to ScyllaDB, behind a new data-services layer.

Stripe's account of moving hundreds of millions of subscription objects states the method most teams use and the constraint that makes it hard: the migration had to run with every service at full traffic and with users expecting consistency throughout. The four-step dual-writing pattern is the answer, one codebase-wide change at a time.

blocks.title: The four-step dual-writing migration, as Stripe describes it
items: Dual write: every new write goes to the existing table and the new one, so they stay in sync; then backfill the missing history into the new table, in Stripe's case hundreds of millions of subscription objects, until the two hold identical information.
Change every read path in the codebase to read from the new table.
Change every write path in the codebase to write only to the new table.
Remove the old data that relies on the outdated data model.

blocks.text: The trap is the cost of the choice that forces this, not the migration itself. A store chosen by preference rather than by the access pattern tends to be left at the worst time, when the dataset is largest and the product busiest. The defence is Discord's: choose the store for the questions you have, but from day one keep the application's data access behind a narrow interface, keep ids and keys that any store can use, and know what the next store will be and what number triggers the move.
Write the exit before the entry. When a store is chosen, record the limit at which it stops fitting, the store that replaces it, and the dual-write plan.

blocks.text: The neutral decision comes first; the product mapping is the last step. On AWS the database decision guide gives it in one table: each managed engine, its data model, when to use it and what it is optimised for. blocks.text: Vector search is where the guide argues most clearly from team familiarity. Rather than a separate vector database, it lists vector capability inside the existing services, ranked by latency and fit, and advises a team that already runs relational databases to evaluate the vector extension on the engine it has before adding a new system.

blocks.text: Map, do not re-decide. The store kind was chosen from the access pattern above; on AWS pick the managed form of that kind, prefer the engine the team already runs for a new capability, and treat the guide's use-when text as the citation for the choice in a design review.

worked_example.title: Worked example: choosing the stores for the news feed

blocks.text: The news feed exercise in this module sizes a product with 10 million daily active users, where each user follows about 200 accounts. Its estimates are the inputs here; every number is an assumption from that exercise, not a measurement. The decision is made per access pattern, and the stores are then counted.

blocks.title: From the access patterns to the stores
items: Posts: 230 creates per second at peak. Any durable store serves this; the posts table and its author index stay relational, because posts are also read by id, edited, deleted and joined to their authors.

Home timeline reads: 11,600 per second at peak, each wanting the newest entries for one user. A sorted list per key, read by range: a wide-column partition or an in-memory capped list, not a relational query that sorts at read time.
Fan-out appends: 46,000 per second at peak, each adding one entry to one follower's list. Write-heavy, by key, eventually consistent: the same per-key list, on a store that makes appends cheap.

Timeline size: 800 entries per user at 16 bytes is 12.8 kB, and the cache for all active users is about 128 GB; an in-memory store holds it, with the wide-column store or a rebuild from the posts table behind it.

Social graph: who follows whom, read when a post is created to find its followers and when a timeline is rebuilt. One hop, by user id: a key-value or relational table, not a graph database, because no question walks further than one hop.
Search: posts by text, low rate, ranked by relevance. A search index derived from the posts table through its change stream, rebuildable, never the only copy.
Media: images and video, large and immutable. An object store, with the media id and attributes in the posts row.
Metrics: the fan-out lag, the cache hit ratio and the request latencies, at a high ingest rate and queried by range. A monitoring time-series store, approximate by design.

Count: one relational primary as the source of truth, one in-memory timeline cache, one wide-column or list store for timelines, one derived search index, one object store and one metrics store, each with a query the primary could not serve at that rate or shape.

ElastiCache in front of Keyspaces or DynamoDB

blocks.text: The decision that changes the architecture is the timeline. If it were kept relational, every home timeline read would sort and merge posts from about 200 followed accounts at 11,600 requests per second, and the choice of fan-out on write would be pointless. Everything else in the table is a derived store that earns its place with one query shape; the relational primary stays the only source of truth, and each derived store can be rebuilt from it.
